name: Gum depigmentation

lead: Gum depigmentation lightens gums that are dark because of melanin, whether from genetics or smoking, for a pinker, more even gumline and a brighter-looking smile.

Pigmented surface tissue is removed or ablated by scalpel, laser or chemical agents, and the gum heals with new, lighter tissue. Published trials are mostly small and compare techniques such as scalpel surgery, diode and Er,Cr:YSGG lasers, microsurgery, bur-based methods and microneedling.

paras: It is a cosmetic periodontal procedure done by a dentist, with the colour change visible after healing. Technique choice affects recovery, and laser-treated gums heal by secondary intention.
Recovery is longer after scalpel surgery, and chemical methods can have side effects. Pigment recurrence is reported inconsistently.

chain: Dark gum layer is removed or bleached
Smile looks brighter and more even
angle.text: People with dark, melanin-pigmented gums have them lightened by scalpel, laser or chemical methods for a more even pink gumline. The new lighter tissue shows once the gums heal, and the studies so far are small technique comparisons.

lead: Gum depigmentation is a cosmetic periodontal procedure that lightens dark, melanin-pigmented gums, using a scalpel, laser or chemical methods.[1] People have it done so that the gum line looks pink and even when they smile, which a 2026 review notes matters particularly for people with a high smile line who show a lot of gum.[2]

Wikipedia notes that gum pigmentation is mainly linked to genetics and tobacco smoking (smoker's melanosis), with melanin made by melanocytes in the basal layer of the gum.[1] A 2018 review describes pigmented gums as an esthetic matter that can also carry psychological negativity for the person, and notes that a wide range of techniques exists.[3]

Published research includes several systematic reviews and a growing set of randomized trials, mostly small, comparing scalpel surgery, diode, CO2, Er:YAG and Er,Cr:YSGG lasers, cryosurgery, microsurgery, bur-based methods, microneedling and injected vitamin C.[4][5][6][7][8][9][2]
infobox: Scalpel, laser, cryosurgery, bur, microneedling, injected vitamin C[1][12][8][9][2]

paras: Gum colour comes from melanin made by melanocytes in the basal layer of the gum epithelium. Wikipedia attributes pigmentation mainly to genetics and to tobacco smoking, which causes smoker's melanosis.[1] Physiological, ethnicity-related pigmentation is common and is treated for how it looks.[7][10]
For smokers, Wikipedia cites a study in which most patients had lost the pigmentation about three months after quitting.[1]

Wikipedia describes laser ablation of melanin-producing cells, scalpel removal of the pigmented layer by a periodontist or oral surgeon, and chemical methods that it says are used less today because of possible side effects.[1] Laser-treated gums heal by secondary intention.[1]

A 2014 systematic review listed bur abrasion, scalpel surgery, cryosurgery, electrosurgery, gingival grafts and lasers as the main options.[8] Lasers reported include CO2, diode, Nd:YAG, Er:YAG and Er,Cr:YSGG types.[11] Newer approaches under study include microneedling with topical agents and injected or topical vitamin C, which is of interest for its role in inhibiting melanin production.[12][13][14][2]

Wikipedia reports that laser treatment gives lighter, more uniform gum colour, that scalpel removal takes longer to heal, and that one Er,Cr:YSGG laser study showed no re-pigmentation at six months; the article is flagged for disputed neutrality and weak sourcing.[1]

Repigmentation is the main long-term question. The 2014 review, based mainly on case reports across 61 publications, found a wide range of recurrence rates between methods and reported low rates for cryosurgery (0.32 percent), electrosurgery (0.74 percent) and laser (1.16 percent).[8] A 2018 review reported that cryosurgery followed by lasers had been described as giving better esthetic results with lower recurrence, while calling for randomized longitudinal trials.[3] A randomized multicenter trial compared the longevity of results after diode, CO2 and Er:YAG laser depigmentation.[15]

For Er:YAG, a literature review found safe, effective depigmentation with significant esthetic improvement, while noting that studies use very different laser settings and different criteria for recurrence.[11]

The 2019 meta-analysis of 25 studies (17 randomized) found laser ablation and surgical stripping did not differ significantly for recurrence or depigmentation achieved, but laser was associated with significantly less postoperative pain.[7] Researchers have also studied topical argan oil, and coenzyme Q10 with vitamin C, as aids to healing after depigmentation.[16][17]

The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis included 25 human trials, mostly of lasers with scalpel surgery as the control; most found no difference between methods, and the meta-analysis showed no significant difference in recurrence (P = 0.75) or depigmentation (P = 0.23) between laser and scalpel, with less pain after laser.[7]

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of six studies compared cryosurgery with laser, blade and abrasion for physiological gingival pigmentation; its abstract reports that laser and scalpel treatments had better therapeutic outcomes than cryosurgery.[9] A 2026 review of eight studies examined vitamin C as a stand-alone or combined treatment.[2]

Randomized trials include a split-mouth comparison of 940 nm ablative and 445 nm non-ablative laser depigmentation in 30 participants aged 18 to 35,[18] a 42-patient trial of injected vitamin C against surgical depigmentation in ethnicity-related hyperpigmentation,[10] a split-mouth vitamin C versus scalpel trial,[19] a split-mouth trial of a ceramic trimming bur,[20] and a comparison of Er,Cr:YSGG laser with surgical stripping with 12 months of follow-up.[21]

Registered trials include a 40-patient comparison of surgical stripping with an Er,Cr:YSGG laser,[4] comparisons of microsurgery with diode laser or conventional scalpel techniques,[5][22] a test of ceramic trimming burs against scalpel,[6] and ongoing trials of microneedling with silymarin or platelet-rich plasma and of vitamin C or glutathione.[12][13][14]

timeline.event: Systematic review of 61 publications compares recurrence across depigmentation methods.[8]
Randomized comparison of Er,Cr:YSGG laser and surgical stripping with 12-month follow-up published.[21]
Meta-analysis of 25 trials finds no significant difference in recurrence between laser and scalpel.[7]
